titre: The Colonial Border That Became a State Border
accroche: In 1810, then again in 1964, two continents choose the same rule to avoid war at independence: keep the inherited borders, exactly as they are.
contenu_vulgarise:
In December 1986, the International Court of Justice must settle a border dispute between Burkina Faso and Mali, two states independent for less than thirty years. The two countries nonetheless agree on the method: find the administrative boundary that French colonization had drawn between Upper Volta and French Sudan, and treat it as-is as the international border. The Court hands down its judgment on December 22, 1986, under the presidency of Judge Mohamed Bedjaoui and with two ad hoc judges, François Luchaire and Georges Abi-Saab: the colonial line, even poorly documented, prevails over the effective occupation of the land by either party.

## A principle recycled more than a century after its creation

The principle the Court applies bears a Latin name from Roman law, uti possidetis juris (“as you possess, so you may possess”), and it was not invented for Africa. It is born in South America between 1810 and 1825, as the Spanish colonies declare their independence one after another. To keep each new border from being settled by force of arms, the jurists of independence, Simón Bolívar among them, adopt the administrative boundaries of the Spanish empire (the viceroyalties, the captaincies general) as they existed in 1810, and turn them into borders between sovereign states.

On July 21, 1964, at its first ordinary session, held in Cairo, the Organization of African Unity adopts resolution AHG/Res.16(I), which declares that all member states pledge to respect the borders existing at the moment they achieve independence. Nothing indicates that its drafters referred to the South American precedent: the solution is found again, not copied. Twenty-two years later, in the case of Burkina Faso v. Mali, the International Court of Justice raises this regional practice to the rank of a general principle of international law.

## What the repetition reveals

One hundred fifty-four years separate the two continents. What this double appearance reveals is that the problem is structural, not regional: with each wave of decolonization, the temptation to redraw borders along lines of ethnicity, geography, or conquest threatens to turn every independence into a conflict between neighbors. Keeping an inherited line, even an arbitrary one, even one drawn in haste by the previous administration, apparently costs less than redrawing it. Here the law does not choose the fairest solution; it chooses the most stable, and makes that stability a value in itself. This is also why the Court upholds the principle even when the colonial boundary invoked is attested only by maps or incomplete administrators' reports: better an uncertain line that is fixed than a border reopened at every dispute.

repere.texte: One hundred fifty-four years separate the adoption of the principle in South America, around 1810, from its adoption by the Organization of African Unity on July 21, 1964. The International Court of Justice raises it to a general principle of international law on December 22, 1986.
repere.source: Resolution AHG/Res.16(I) of the Organization of African Unity, adopted in Cairo on July 21, 1964; International Court of Justice, Frontier Dispute (Burkina Faso/Republic of Mali), judgment of December 22, 1986

carte.punch: The same rule fixed the borders of South America in 1810, then of Africa in 1964.
carte.idee: To keep independence from being settled by war, the South American jurists of 1810, then the Organization of African Unity in 1964, keep the administrative borders inherited from colonization. In 1986, the International Court of Justice makes it a general principle.
carte.source_courte: ICJ, Burkina Faso v. Mali, Dec. 22, 1986

quiz.question: Why does the International Court of Justice uphold the colonial administrative boundary rather than effective occupation of the land in the case of Burkina Faso v. Mali?
choix: Because French colonial law remains applicable to former colonies after their independence
Because Mali and Burkina Faso had signed a bilateral treaty fixing this border before 1986
Because fixing borders on inherited boundaries keeps every independence from turning into an armed conflict between neighbors
Because the United Nations imposes this principle on every new member state
quiz.explication: The principle of uti possidetis juris aims to stabilize new states, not to extend colonial law or to meet a UN obligation: by freezing inherited boundaries, it takes away their status as a stake and keeps territorial dispute from adding to the tensions of independence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where, and by whom, is the principle of uti possidetis juris first formulated, before its adoption in Africa?
choix: In South America, between 1810 and 1825, by jurists including Simón Bolívar
By the French colonial administration, in the 19th century
By the League of Nations, after World War I
By the Organization of African Unity itself, in 1964
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The principle is born in South America between 1810 and 1825, when the jurists of independence, Simón Bolívar among them, adopt the Spanish administrative boundaries as borders.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Did the drafters of the 1964 Organization of African Unity resolution draw on the South American precedent?
choix: Yes, the resolution explicitly cites Simón Bolívar in its preamble
Yes, a South American delegate proposed the text at the Cairo summit
Nothing indicates it: the solution is found again, not copied from the precedent
No, they devised an entirely different mechanism
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that nothing indicates the resolution's drafters referred to the South American precedent: the solution is found again, not copied.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role does the quality of colonial documentation play in the International Court of Justice's 1986 judgment?
choix: Incomplete documentation leads the Court to set aside the colonial boundary
The Court requires the unanimous agreement of neighboring states before ruling
The Court orders a new topographical survey before deciding
The Court upholds the principle even if the boundary is attested only by incomplete documents
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the Court upholds the principle even when the colonial boundary is attested only by incomplete documents, a fixed line being worth more than a border reopened.
